newsitem.title: UK: Carmakers use surreal ads to escape look-alikes.
newsitem.headline: Carmakers use surreal ads to escape look-alikes.

text.p: Car companies that are trying to avoid look-alike television commercials are spending lots of money on glitzy, surreal advertising that sometimes doesn't even show cars.
Industry experts say a growing number of car ads in places like the United States and Britain no longer focus on technical details but on the "personality" of the brand.

Last year 500 million pounds ($810 million) was spent on advertising cars on TV in Britain. The images used are becoming increasingly surreal in a bid to attract the attention of viewers blitzed by look-alike campaigns.
British car ads have traditionally featured a winding road, beautiful scenery, a glamorous couple and haunting soundtrack with some technical detail thrown in for good measure.
"Because it is all aspirational much of the advertising is overtly status-ridden and packed with sterotypes," a spokesman for ad agency Publicis which runs the Renault account told Reuters.
But things are changing.
Ford's latest campaign for its Fiesta brand includes shots of an old man bouncing on a trampoline and a man blowing a bubble-gum bubble. It offers only a glimpse of the car in the final frame.
The launch campaign for Ford's Ka marque last year showed a lighthouse, a pair of feet and a bumble bee but no car.
Simon Binns, account director at Ford's ad agency Ogilvy & Mather said, "To appeal to ad literate (consumers) the advertising had to be incredibly fresh and original."

It is a tactic that has also been adopted by Germany's BMW which has run a print ad featuring a yellow rubber duck with the BMW logo instead of eyes and by Japan's Nissan, which according to a recent report in the Wall Street Journal, ran a TV ad in the U.S. with no sign of the vehicles it is trying to promote.
Ad agencies are increasingly using this approach because there is little to distinguish one car brand from another.

"Cars are becoming more and more similar. The technical differences are fewer and fewer and so the perceived image of the car becomes the biggest differentiating factor," said Chris Wood, chairman of branding company CLK.
His view is supported by Simon Mottram, a director of international branding group Interbrand.
"It's a huge trend for car makers to put personality into their brands. Cars used to be sold on their functional aspects. Now it's all about softer more expressive values," he said.

The Mini car brand, which is made by Rover and which achieved cult status in the 1960s, is to be promoted as a fashion accessory in British style magazines this summer. The ads will feature a range of brightly coloured customised cars which are almost hidden against a bright background.

"The Mini is a very individual brand and we want to emphasise that. If you drive one you can be cool, or trendy, or sporty or classic -- it allows you to express your own personality," said Paul Gordon account director on the Mini brand at ad agency Ammirati Puris Lintas.
Gordon said that the Mini has also achieved cult status in Japan. "It is seen as quirky and quintessentially English."

While some British car ads have taken a surreal turn to promote the personality of the brand, others are pastiches of popular TV shows or glitzy Hollywood movies. An ad for the Nissan Almera parodies the 1970s British police series "The Sweeney" and another for the Peugoet 106, has a story line loosely based on the movie "Thelma and Louise".
Ad industry experts say that while the ads are entertaining, many consumers have trouble remembering the product being advertised.

"We have found in research groups that although consumers enjoy the advertising they often can't remember who it was for. Which rather defeats the object," said Janet Bik, a director of branding specialist New Solutions.

Dave Trott, creative director of ad agency Walsh Trott Chick Smith recently said in an interview with the Daily Mail, "Do you remember the car ad with the soundtrack 'Search for the hero'? Beautifully shot, nicely edited, terrific song. But what was it for? Several million pounds later and all you're thinking is great soundtrack."
Trott said the problem with the ad for Peugoet and many others is "the advertisement becomes an end in itself and the selling of the product is forgotten."

Nissan's U.S. ad campaign was well received by the public but sales fell, the Wall Street Journal Europe reportedly recently. It was only when the company introduced a discounting policy last year that it met sales targets.
Some industry experts believe car companies will return to concentrating on branding and on technical features and will show their cars in ads.
New Solutions Bik said, "I think they (carmakers) will begin to tie the imagery more closely with the brand and use the car as the central hero of ad campaigns."
"Ironically as car dealerships consolidate and their numbers decline, ads will be one of the places where consumers will actually be able to see what the cars look like," she said.
